query: What kappa/ICC thresholds and double-coding percentages are recommended for low-frequency or ambiguous multimodal categories in CA corpora?

response.query: What kappa/ICC thresholds and double-coding percentages are recommended for low-frequency or ambiguous multimodal categories in CA corpora?
response.answer: For low-frequency or ambiguous multimodal categories, kappa/ICC thresholds below 0.4 are often considered problematic, and double-coding percentages above 80% are recommended for reliability.

results.title: Multimodal Corpora | CLARIN ERIC - Common Language Resources and Technology Infrastructure
results.content: # Multimodal Corpora. Multimodal corpora are data collections used to study how two or more modalities interface with one another in human communication. In this sense, multimodal corpora are often collections of video and speech recordings accompanied with transcriptions and gesture annotations, although multimodal corpora of textual data supplemented with images exist as well. Such corpora can be used for “the exploration of a range of lexical, prosodic and gestural features of conversation, and for investigations of the ways in which these features interact in real, everyday speech (Abuczki and Baiat Ghazaleh 2013: 88). The CLARIN infrastructure offers 17 multimodal corpora, 13 of which are monolingual (English, Estonian, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Hungarian, Italian, Slovenian, and Zulu). These corpora are richly annotated for various verbal and non-verbal elements of communication, such as body gesture, gaze direction, and head, eye, and lip movement. **For comments, changes of the existing content or inclusion of new corpora, send us an**resource-families [at] clarin.eu (**email**)**.**. ## The Multimodal Corpora in the CLARIN Infrastructure. ### Video-Audio Corpora. ### Text-Image Corpora. results.title: Multimodal Language Corpora Workshop | UCL Faculty of Brain Sciences
results.content: The Multimodal Language Corpora Workshop brought together researchers sharing a strong interest in communication and conversation in real-world settings. Researchers from psychology, cognitive neuroscience, linguistics and computer science working on multimodal corpora explored questions related to social interaction, language development, language production, comprehension, linguistic structure and use. The corpora presented differed along many dimensions, including size, availability, characteristics of the people (and how many) being recorded, the language spoken/signed, the “task”, and what has been annotated. The British Sign Language (BSL) Corpus is the first corpus of its kind in the United Kingdom (i.e., a large machine-readable open access dataset that is maximally representative of the language) and one of the largest sign language corpora in the world. British Sign Language Corpus Project: A corpus of digital video data and annotations of British Sign Language 2008-2014 (Second Edition). The ECOLANG corpus provides audiovisual recordings (about 25 mins each) and annotation of multimodal behaviours (speech transcription, gesture, object manipulation, and eye gaze) by British and US English-speaking adults engaged in semi-naturalistic conversation with their child (N = 38, children 3-4 years old) or a familiar adult (N = 32). To demonstrate what opportunities FreMIC’s (combination of) transcriptions, annotations, and multmodal data opens up for research in Interactional (Corpus) Linguistics, this paper reports on a study on pupillary responses in selected vs. The Language Development Project (LDP) corpus represents a significant resource for researchers exploring language acquisition, cognitive development, and multimodal communication. The aims of this presentation are: (a) to briefly introduce the MultiModal MultiDimensional (M3D) gesture coding system, (b) to present two multimodal corpora that have been manually annotated in accordance with M3D principles, namely the "Audiovisual corpus of Catalan children’s narrative discourse development" (Vilà-Giménez et al., 2023, ) and the M3D-TED corpus (Rohrer et al., 2023, ); and (c) to discuss the annotation of the corpora and their potential future uses. The corpus contains approximately one hour of annotated multimodal speech and includes speech transcriptions, annotations for gesture (M3D), information structure (LISA guidelines; Götze, 2007), and full ToBI annotations for speech prosody for each language.

results.title: New trends in corpora and language learning , by A. Frankenberg ...
results.content: Unlike other similar reports on corpora for translation, her study highlights the merits of general monolingual corpora in this ﬁeld as she claims that a general monolingual corpus can help students ﬁnd correct collocations, colligations, semantic preferences and The ﬁnal chapter in this part, by Kaszubski, introduces IF AConc ( edu.pl/~ifaconc), an online pedagogic concordancing tool helping students to “explore, gather, annotate, discuss and share facts of usage pertaining to their language needs as This chapter, as is stated in the introduction of the book, could have been included in the “tools” section. The common mode for carrying out such studies is to investi- gate different frequency distributions of linguistic items among these corpora, to reveal the overuse and underuse of linguistic features in a non-native or learner corpus as compared In such studies, traditional hypotheses or categories of language, such as word and parts of speech, are often applied as the basis of comparison. former, corpora are used only to “expound, test or exemplify theories and descriptions that were formulated before large corpora became availab le to inform language study” 65), while in the latter, the aim is to “deri ve linguistic categories systematically from the recurrent patterns and the frequency distributions that emerge from language in context” The corpus-driven approach has led to quite a few new corpus-linguistic categories, such as the prefabricated unit, lexical item, (extended) unit of meaning, cluster, colligation, collocation, semantic preference, semantic association and semantic prosody. Compared with How to Use Corpora in Language T eaching (2004), edited by Sinclair, which focused on raising the aw areness about the potential uses and beneﬁts of using corpora in language teaching, this volume has shifted the emphasis to the extended uses of corpora in diverse areas with regard to language education, the incorporation of new corpus-linguistic theories or categories into the applications of language learning, the development of more advanced corpus tools to facilitate language learning based on these theories as well as corpus technology, and the application of new emergent multimodal corpora to language pedagogy.
